title: Likes and dislikes
goal: Express likes, dislikes, and opinions — and see why Dutch "like" has several forms that can't stand in for each other.
bekal: telling apart *houden van*, *leuk vinden*, *lekker vinden*, and *graag*
giving your opinion with *ik vind* and *volgens mij*
wave: Go back to **unit 14**: write a ten-item shopping list with all the amounts, then read it out as if you were standing at the counter.

dialogs.title: Dialog — Wat vind jij?
dialogs.intro: Dinner at Sanne's place. There's one dish that, to Budi, needs some explaining.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ik weet het nog niet. Wat zit erin?
lines.id: I don't know yet. What's in it?
lines.literal: I know it still not. what sits in-it?

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Aardappels, boerenkool en een worst erbovenop.
lines.id: Potatoes, kale, and a sausage on top.
lines.literal: potatoes, farmer's-cabbage and a sausage on-it.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: En dat eten jullie in de winter?
lines.id: And you eat that in winter?
lines.literal: and that eat you(pl) in the winter?

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Elke week. Mijn moeder vindt het heerlijk.
lines.id: Every week. My mother loves it.
lines.literal: every week. my mother finds it delicious.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nee hoor! Ik eet graag nieuwe dingen. Maar ik mis sambal.
lines.id: Not at all! I like trying new things. I just miss sambal.
lines.literal: no really! I eat gladly new things. but I miss sambal.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Sambal bij stamppot? Dat doet mijn oma ook.
lines.id: Sambal on stamppot? My grandma does that too.
lines.literal: sambal on stamppot? that does my grandma also.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Ze woonde jaren in Indonesië. Ze houdt meer van sambal dan ik.
lines.id: She lived in Indonesia for years. She likes sambal more than I do.
lines.literal: she lived years in Indonesia. she holds more of sambal than I.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Dan vind ik jullie familie meteen een stuk leuker.
lines.id: Then I like your family a whole lot more already.
lines.literal: then find I your family right-away a piece more-fun.

notes: **Hou je van…?** — *houden van* is literally "hold of", but it means to like sincerely, even to love. *Ik hou* (not *ik houd*) is the everyday form.
**Wat zit erin?** — *zitten* again (unit 14), plus *erin* (in it). This is the sentence for asking what's in a dish.
**Stamppot** — mashed potatoes mixed with vegetables, the most typical Dutch winter dish. The version with *boerenkool* (kale) is the most famous.
**Mijn moeder vindt het heerlijk** — *vinden* means "to find" **and** "to think, be of the opinion". It's the main verb for giving opinions: *Ik vind het mooi*, *Wat vind jij?*

**Ik vind het… interessant** — and Sanne is right. In Dutch social life, *interessant* is often a polite way of saying "I don't like it", much like an English speaker's "interesting…". The Dutch are known for being blunt, but they have their own subtle codes too.
**Ik eet graag nieuwe dingen** — *graag* + verb = to like doing something. It's the most common way to say you like an **activity**, and the one beginners forget most.
**Ik mis sambal** — *missen* means both to miss someone/something and to miss (a train), just as in English.

**Ze woonde jaren in Indonesië** — the past tense, which awaits you in the next units. The Dutch-Indonesian connection makes sentences like this common: many Dutch families have a grandmother who grew up on Java or Sumatra.

grammars.title: Several ways to say "like"
body: English mostly gets by with "like" and "love". Dutch chooses according to **what** you like.
after: ⚠️ *Ik hou van kaas* sounds over the top — as if cheese were the love of your life. For food, use *lekker vinden*.
⚠️ *Ik hou van voetballen* is odd too; for activities use *graag*: *Ik voetbal graag.*
The negatives: *Ik hou niet van…*, *Ik vind het niet leuk*, *Ik lees niet graag*. For real dislike: *Ik heb een hekel aan…* (I hate…).

grammars.title: Giving your opinion
body: The Dutch see a direct opinion as honesty, not rudeness — but they still have phrases to soften it.

head: Nederlands
English
rows: Ik ben het er niet mee eens.
It's not as bad as all that.

after: *Ik vind dat…* and *Ik denk dat…* are followed by a subordinate clause, where the verb moves to the end: *Ik vind dat het te duur **is**.* That's unit 20 — for now, you can stop before *dat*: *Ik vind het te duur.*
*Dat klopt* (that's right, that adds up) is one of the most frequent Dutch sentences; the negative is *dat klopt niet*.
Dutch honesty can be sharp: if your presentation wasn't great, you'll be told straight out. It isn't personal rejection — and because their praise is rare, it means something.

blocks.title: What the Dutch actually do in their free time
items: **Fietsen** isn't a sport but a way of getting around — though *een fietstocht* (a bike ride) on the weekend is a real outing.
**Wandelen** — long walks in nature, with proper shoes and a planned route. Seen as a full activity, not just a stroll.
**Klussen** — fixing up and remodeling your own home. Hardware stores are packed every Saturday morning.
**Verjaardagsfeestje** — a birthday party with guests seated in a circle, coffee, and cake. Famous worldwide for its circle of chairs.
**Op vakantie** — vacations are planned months ahead, often with a camper.

head: Nederlands
English
rows: Wat doe je graag in je vrije tijd?
What do you like doing in your free time?
Ik lees graag / Ik kook graag.
I like reading / I like cooking.
Wat voor muziek vind je mooi?
What kind of music do you like?
Ik vind het niet zo leuk.
Ik heb een hekel aan wachten.

blocks.text: *Gek zijn op* (literally: be crazy on) is the most enthusiastic way to say you like something, and it's safe for both food and activities: *Ik ben gek op stroopwafels.*

*Wat voor …?* means "what kind of": *Wat voor werk doe je?*, *Wat voor muziek luister je?* It can split up in longer sentences — *Wat voor een boek is dat?* — and it's very handy for taking a conversation deeper.
